headline: High: shared filesystem and broad write/network defaults create prompt-injection, leakage, and cascading-error risks between Continue and ms-swift.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Continue can read/write workspace files and use MCP; ms-swift can read/write files and run CLI/Python workflows. The pair shares state via filesystem in Continue’s model, so attacker-controlled content from one can be consumed by the other. No direct clipboard or message-queue bridge is documented, so this is inferred rather than observed.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same workspace or dataset directory
IF either agent parses file contents as instructions or tool directives
mitigations: Separate the agents into different directories
Disable MCP servers for Continue unless needed
Use read-only mounts for ms-swift inputs
Add provenance labels to shared files
requires-engineering: add content-sanitization before either agent ingests peer-generated files

B_data_leakage.rationale: Continue touches source code and open editor buffers, while ms-swift touches datasets, checkpoints, logs, and configuration files. Because Continue shares state via filesystem and both have filesystem access, sensitive material can cross between them in default workspace setups. The exact data path is not directly documented, so uncertainty keeps this at medium rather than high.
conditions: IF the same filesystem tree contains source code and training artifacts
IF either agent writes logs or outputs into a shared directory
mitigations: Use separate workspaces per agent
Exclude secrets and checkpoints from shared mounts
Rotate or redact logs before sharing them
Restrict Continue to editor buffers only
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent filesystem ACLs

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents have unrestricted filesystem write and subprocess execution, and Continue explicitly shares state via filesystem. ms-swift also writes datasets, models, checkpoints, and logs. Concurrent writes to the same directory can overwrite each other or corrupt artifacts; no locking is documented for either agent, so the safer choice is high.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same writable directory
IF either agent performs concurrent file generation or cleanup
mitigations: Assign disjoint output directories
Serialize runs with a manual lock file
Make one agent read-only on shared inputs
Back up mutable artifacts before execution
requires-engineering: add transactional writes or locking

D_cascading_error.rationale: Continue can produce code or edits from workspace context, and ms-swift can consume files, logs, and configuration data in CLI/Python workflows. If ms-swift treats Continue’s output as authoritative, errors can propagate into training or evaluation artifacts. There is no direct evidence of verification steps, so the interaction is plausible but not proven.
conditions: IF ms-swift ingests Continue-generated files without review
IF Continue-generated code or configs are used as training or evaluation inputs
mitigations: Require human review before reuse
Add checksum or schema validation
Keep generated artifacts in a quarantine folder
Compare outputs against a baseline run
requires-engineering: add automated verification gates

E_compliance.rationale: Continue is an IDE assistant handling source code and editor buffers, while ms-swift handles datasets, checkpoints, logs, and configuration data. That creates a plausible retention and residency mismatch if regulated data is placed into shared files or logs. No specific HIPAA/GDPR certification data is provided for either agent, so the risk is compliance-process mismatch rather than a proven breach.
conditions: IF regulated data is stored in shared workspace files or logs
IF retention or deletion policies differ between the two toolchains
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of shared directories
Redact logs before retention
Document a single retention policy for both tools
Verify residency requirements before deployment
requires-engineering: implement policy-based data routing
